hero.subtitle: Three popular ATS platforms used by tech companies — but their hidden mechanics determine whether your application surfaces or sinks.
hero.direct_answer: Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby do not use secret auto-reject scores that bury qualified developers. Recruiters primarily see candidates sorted by application date and pipeline stage, then apply keyword searches and filters on parsed profiles. Greenhouse excels at structured parsing and scorecards; Lever emphasizes full-text search and CRM nurturing; Ashby leverages AI summaries and customizable analytics. Understanding each system's parsing and recruiter workflow is key to bypassing filters and landing in the right pipeline stage.

content_html:
Why Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby Matter in 2026

Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby power hiring at thousands of tech companies, from startups to scale-ups. For web developers, these ATS platforms control visibility. Recruiters don’t manually review every resume. They rely on parsed data, pipeline stages, and targeted searches. Misunderstand the mechanics and your tailored application disappears into the void.

Real pain points from developer forums and recruiter discussions show applications vanishing due to poor parsing or mismatched keywords. This post breaks down the actual filter mechanics based on official behaviors and practitioner insights. [[IMAGE:comparison-diagram]]

No magic score rejects you automatically. But failing to appear in recruiter searches does the same thing.

[[CTA:mid]]

How Greenhouse Filters and Processes Candidates

Greenhouse does not auto-reject based on a hidden score. Recruiters see a pipeline view sorted primarily by application date within stages like Application Review. They use structured scorecards, keyword filters, and parsed fields to evaluate candidates.

Parsing is sophisticated. Greenhouse extracts skills, experience, and education into structured fields. Recruiters search these fields or use custom questions as knockout filters. Clean, standard-formatted resumes parse best — preferably DOCX with clear section headers (Experience, Skills). Multi-column layouts or non-standard dates often break extraction.

Pipeline Stages and Recruiter View

Applications land in Application Review. Recruiters advance strong ones to Recruiter Screen or assessments. Scorecards map directly to job requirements. Your parsed profile populates these, making precise skill mentions and quantified achievements critical.

Internal links to other posts: optimize for Workday pipeline stages similarly.

Lever’s Full-Text Search and CRM Mechanics

Lever prioritizes recruiter search across full resume text and tags. No dominant auto-score; candidates appear in pipelines sorted by date or custom filters. Strong CRM features let recruiters nurture passive talent.

Parsing stores the full document for broad keyword matching. Recruiters tag candidates and filter by skills, location, or previous interactions. Detailed, achievement-focused bullets improve relevance in searches. Cover letters can help flag high-potential profiles.

Key Differences for Developers

Lever surfaces candidates via keyword density and semantic matches, especially post-Gem AI integrations for ranking suggestions. Mirror job description language naturally without stuffing.

[[IMAGE:lever-parsing]]

Ashby’s AI-Driven Summaries and Custom Views

Ashby offers highly customizable recruiter dashboards with AI-assisted summaries and criteria matching. Default views are flexible; recruiters build filters based on job requirements. AI helps generate candidate overviews highlighting fit.

Parsing benefits from clear, quantified content. AI emphasizes results over keywords alone. Short application forms focus attention on your CV and portfolio. Take-homes often serve as the real filter after initial review.

Analytics and Rediscovery Features

Ashby shines in data-driven hiring with reports and talent rediscovery. Past strong candidates get resurfaced via AI. Make your profile memorable with specific impacts that AI can match to new roles.

faq.question: Do Greenhouse, Lever, or Ashby use hidden scores to auto-reject candidates?
faq.answer: No. None of these platforms default to a single hidden rejection score visible to recruiters. They sort by application date and pipeline stage. Recruiters then search and filter parsed data. Automated elements assist but humans decide advances.

faq.question: Which format works best for resumes across these ATS?
faq.answer: DOCX generally parses most reliably, especially for Greenhouse. Use standard headings, clear dates (Month Year), and single-column layouts. Avoid tables, headers/footers, and graphics that break extraction. Test with tools where possible.

faq.question: How important are keywords vs. achievements in these systems?
faq.answer: Keywords help discovery in searches, but achievements and structure matter more for human review and AI summaries. Mirror job description language naturally. Quantify impacts to stand out in scorecards or AI matches.

faq.question: Can I check my application status in these ATS?
faq.answer: Limited visibility. Greenhouse may offer a candidate portal with basic status. Lever and Ashby provide little to no candidate-facing tracking. Silence after 2-3 weeks often signals no movement.

conclusion.summary_html:
Greenhouse favors structured, scorable profiles. Lever rewards searchable, detailed content and relationships. Ashby leverages AI clarity and customization. Master the mechanics common to all — clean parsing and relevance — while adapting per platform. The real differentiator remains demonstrating genuine fit through your work.

Stop guessing which filters you pass. Let AI matching surface opportunities that align.
